stem.text: Two polar curves are given by \( r = 3 \theta \sin{\left(\theta \right)} + 10 \) and \( r = 3 \cos{\left(\theta \right)} + 2 \) for \( 0 \le \theta \le \frac{\pi}{2} \), and they do not meet on this interval. Let D be the distance between the two curves measured along the ray at angle \( \theta \). Using a calculator, find the rate at which D changes with respect to \( \theta \) at \( \theta = 0.5 \). Show the setup, and give the value correct to three decimal places.

worked_solution.text: On the interval \( \theta\sin\theta \ge 0 \), so the first radius is at least 10, while the second is at most 5. The first curve is outside, so \( D(\theta) = 3 \theta \sin{\left(\theta \right)} + 10 - \left(3 \cos{\left(\theta \right)} + 2\right) \).
Differentiate, using the product rule on \( \theta\sin\theta \): \( D'(\theta) = 3 \theta \cos{\left(\theta \right)} + 6 \sin{\left(\theta \right)} \).
At \( \theta = 0.5 \), a calculator in radian mode gives \( D' \approx 4.193 \).

options.derivation: only the outer radius differentiated, so dr/dtheta of the first curve is reported as the rate of the gap
the outer radius differentiated without the product rule, theta sin(theta) giving cos(theta)
the inner curve taken as the outer one, so the gap is written inner minus outer and its derivative has the wrong sign
